title: Process schematic and P&ID: how is the rig built?
summary: A flow diagram of a rig with boxes for equipment, arrows for flow, a symbol for a valve and numbered circles for instruments. It shows what is connected to what, in which direction things flow and where the measurements are taken.

media.alt: Process schematic with fuel tank, pump, valve, vaporizer, burner and exhaust boxes joined by arrows, an air supply and nitrogen purge, and numbered instrument circles.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How is the rig built?
read_the_figure.axes: No axes: left to right is the main process direction. Boxes: equipment (fuel tank, pump, vaporizer, burner, exhaust, air supply). Solid arrows: process line. Dashed rose arrow: purge. Circles with dotted lines: instruments and their signals. Bow-tie symbol: valve V-1.
look_at: What is the path of the fuel from tank to exhaust?
Which instruments measure which equipment, and what do the tags say (TIC 101, PI 102, FI 103, LI 104)?
Where does the second stream (air, purge) enter?
Is there a legend for line types?
read_the_figure.proves: A schematic shows the topology of the rig and what is measured where. It does not show dimensions, materials or the real layout, and it proves nothing about performance.
if_wrong: No legend for dashed or coloured lines: a purge or a signal line is read as a process line.
Tags without a key: TIC and FI mean nothing to a new reader.
Missing valve or purge path: the diagram cannot be used to operate or to check safety.

terms.meaning: Piping and instrumentation diagram: equipment, lines, valves and instruments with tags, drawn in a standard notation.
Letters give the measured variable and function, a number the loop: TIC 101 is a temperature indicating controller, loop 101.
The line that carries the working fluid; drawn solid with an arrowhead for direction.
Dotted line carrying a measurement or control signal, not material.
Inert gas (here nitrogen) used to flush a line before or after use.

remember: Tag letters: T temperature, P pressure, F flow, L level; I indicate, C control.
Solid = process, dashed = purge, dotted = signal. Read the legend.
Flow runs left to right; arrows give the truth.
A schematic has topology, not scale.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Rounded boxes encode equipment, with colour (teal tank, blue pump and air, amber vaporizer, rose burner, grey exhaust) for the role and a bold label for the main units. Arrows encode flow direction, line style encodes the type of line (solid, dashed, dotted), circles are instruments with a tag in two lines, and a bow-tie symbol is a valve. A small legend and a tag key complete the encoding.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A rig is a graph: units are nodes and pipes are edges. A drawing in which position carries order (left to right is the flow) and colour carries role lets a reader trace the path in seconds. The instrument circles tie the measurement to its equipment, so the reader knows what the data in the other figures mean: a temperature trace may come from the vaporizer's TIC 101.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What is the fuel's path? Tank, pump, valve V-1, vaporizer, burner, exhaust. Q2: What is measured and where? TIC 101 on the vaporizer (temperature, with control), PI 102 at the pump (pressure), FI 103 at the burner (flow) and LI 104 on the tank (level); the dotted lines are signal lines. Q3: How do air and purge enter? Air comes from the supply into the bottom of the burner (blue arrow); the N2 purge (rose dashed arrow) goes into the vaporizer from below, and is shown dashed because it is used only for flushing.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Palette from tokens: colours are not free decoration. Using the same token for the same role in every diagram (tank teal, heater amber) means a reader who has learned one figure can read the next. Colours chosen ad hoc lose that.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A schematic is not to scale: the pump and the burner look equal in size but may differ a hundred-fold. Colour is used for category only and should not suggest temperature. A missing safety element (relief valve, check valve) is not noticed because nothing says the drawing is complete. Without a revision date the diagram may not match the rig. Colours that are not from a fixed palette change meaning between figures.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A photograph with labels for what the rig looks like; a 3D CAD view for dimensions; a table of instruments with ranges and uncertainties; a block diagram with energy and mass flows on each line.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add flow rates and temperatures on each line, a line list table, and a relief path to the exhaust.

steps.title: Heat duty of a vaporizer (illustrative)
steps.note: Sensible heat to warm the liquid plus latent heat to vaporise it; this is what TIC 101 must supply.

steps.title: Mass balance on the line
steps.note: Along a single line the flow is the same at every instrument: FI 103 should read the pump's flow.

worked.title: Heater duty for the vaporizer (illustrative numbers)
worked.problem: A liquid fuel at 1 g/s is warmed from 20 C to 80 C (cp = 2.0 kJ/kg/K) and vaporised (h_fg = 400 kJ/kg). What power must the heater supply?

solution.text: Convert the flow and apply the formula.

worked.answer: 0.52 kW, mostly latent heat; the number is only illustrative, not a property of any real fuel.

checks.q: What do the letters in TIC 101 mean?
checks.answer: T = temperature, I = indicating, C = controller; 101 is the loop number.

checks.q: Fuel flow is 2 g/s with cp = 2 kJ/kg/K, dT = 60 K, h_fg = 400 kJ/kg. Power?
FI 103 reads half of the flow the pump delivers. What does the diagram suggest as causes?
checks.hint: Look for branches and signal lines.
checks.answer: Look for a leak, a bypass or a purge branch between pump and burner; on this diagram there is none, so check the instrument calibration first.
